title: Oedipus the King
author: Sophocles
openingText: Suppliants of all ages are seated around the altar at the palace doors, with a PRIEST OF ZEUS at their head. OEDIPUS enters to them.
about:
Thebes is suffering from plague. King Oedipus, who once saved the city from the Sphinx, promises to find the cause. The answer from Delphi points to an unresolved murder: the former king, Laius, was killed, and his killer has not been punished. Oedipus begins an investigation, but the witnesses’ accounts increasingly threaten his understanding of his own life.

Information emerges through arguments, pleas, memories and questioning. Oedipus seeks both the truth and his city’s safety, while suspicion and anger shape how he listens. The chorus’s songs follow the citizens’ changing hopes and fears. This edition presents the dialogue in modern English; the original-English companion preserves Storr’s verse translation.

angleCards.title: The investigation turns on the king
angleCards.text: Follow how each new disclosure changes the meaning of earlier information. Which clues does Oedipus recognize, and which does he misunderstand?
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to trace the connection between the witnesses’ evidence and Oedipus’s changing explanations.

angleCards.title: Knowing more than the characters
angleCards.text: For readers who know the myth, reassuring words can sound like warnings. Watch the gap between what a speaker intends and what an audience can understand.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to examine how dramatic irony changes the meaning of individual speeches.

angleCards.title: Action and fate
angleCards.text: The characters try to avoid the disasters predicted by oracles. Examine their decisions and the knowledge available when they make them.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to distinguish prediction, intention and responsibility without assuming the play offers a simple answer.

angleCards.title: The king and the city
angleCards.text: The murder is a public problem: the oracle connects the city’s suffering to a pollution that must be removed. How does this shape the king’s promises and duties?
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow the relationship between personal guilt, ritual pollution and responsibility for the community.

cast.name: Oedipus
cast.description: He saved the city from the Sphinx and now rules with Jocasta. He wants to find Laius’s killer and save his people, but responds angrily when others challenge him.

cast.name: Jocasta
cast.description: Formerly married to Laius, she is now Oedipus’s wife. She initially tries to reassure him by questioning prophecy, but later begs him to stop his inquiry.

cast.name: Creon
cast.description: He brings the oracle’s answer from Delphi. He defends himself when Oedipus suspects him of seeking power and assumes authority near the play’s end.

cast.name: Teiresias
cast.description: Oedipus summons him for help, but he initially refuses to reveal what he knows. Their conversation turns into a bitter confrontation.

cast.name: Priest of Zeus
cast.description: He describes the city’s suffering and asks Oedipus to save it again. Oedipus has already sent Creon to Delphi when the play begins.

cast.name: Chorus
cast.description: They pray, hope and struggle to understand events. Their songs and questions express both loyalty to the king and fear for his fate.

whyItMatters.title: A discovery that changes everything
whyItMatters.body: The investigation does not create the earlier deeds, but changes what they mean to Oedipus. The play explores how a person’s understanding of himself can collapse when familiar facts acquire a new context.

whyItMatters.title: Responsibility without full knowledge
whyItMatters.body: Oedipus acts without knowing all the identities and relationships his actions involve. The play raises difficult questions about the difference between choosing an act and understanding its full significance.

whyItMatters.title: Words that return to their speaker
whyItMatters.body: Promises, curses and attempts at reassurance carry implications their speakers do not foresee. Language becomes part of the action, rewarding attention to repeated words and double meanings.
